Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 71, verse 5–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I have invited my people night and day. But my invitation has not increased them except in flight."﴾

Know that this is among the verses which indicate that all events occur by the decree (qada') and predestination (qadar) of God. That is because we see two persons hearing the call of the Messenger in one assembly, with one wording. For one of them that speech becomes a cause for the arising of guidance, inclination and desire, while for the second it becomes a cause for increased arrogance and haughtiness, and the utmost aversion. No one may say that this aversion and this desire came about by the choice of the responsible person (mukallaf). For this is obstinacy (mukabarah) against what is perceived by the senses. The one who feels aversion finds his heart as if compelled toward that aversion, and the one who feels desire finds his heart as if compelled toward that desire. And whenever that aversion arises, rebellion and turning away must follow it; and if desire arises, submission and obedience must follow it. So we know that the hearing of that call leading, in the case of one of them, to desire which necessarily entails obedience and submission, and in the case of the second, to aversion which necessarily entails rebellion and disobedience, does not occur except by the decree and predestination of God.

If it is said: Grant that the arising of aversion and desire is not by his choice, yet the occurrence of disobedience at the time of aversion is by his choice, for the servant is able, despite that aversion, to submit and obey. We say: If aversion arose unopposed by any aspect of desire, but purely free of all admixtures of desire, it would be impossible for the act to occur along with it. That is because, at the moment aversion and desire arise, the act does not occur at all. So at the arising of aversion, the absence of the requisite (muqtada) is joined by the presence of an obstacle (mani'), and thus the act becoming impossible is more fitting. Therefore it is established that this verse is among the strongest proofs for qada' and qadar.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 71, verses 7–9:

Then God Most High said: ﴿And indeed, every time I have called them, that You might forgive them﴾.

Know that Noah, peace be upon him, called them to worship (ʿibadah), piety (taqwa) and obedience (taʿah) only so that they might be forgiven. For the first aim is the attainment of forgiveness, while obedience is sought only as a means to attaining forgiveness. Therefore, when he commanded them to worship, he said: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾. Since the first thing sought from the call was the attainment of forgiveness, he said: ﴿And indeed, every time I have called them, that You might forgive them﴾. Know also that when he, peace be upon him, called them, they dealt with him in four ways:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾, meaning that they went so far in imitation (taqlid) that they put their fingers in their ears, so that they would not hear the proof (hujjah) and the clear evidence (bayyinah).

The second is His saying: ﴿And covered themselves with their garments﴾, that is, they wrapped themselves in them. This was either so that they would not see his face, as though they did not allow themselves to hear his words or to see his face; or it was for the sake of intensifying the refusal to hear, for when they put their fingers in their ears and then, in addition, covered themselves with their garments, the barrier to hearing became stronger.

The third is His saying: ﴿And persisted﴾, meaning that they persisted in their way, or in their turning away from hearing the call to the truth.

The fourth is His saying: ﴿And were arrogant with great arrogance﴾, that is, a great arrogance reaching its utmost extreme.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿Then indeed I called them openly﴾ ﴿Then indeed I proclaimed to them and I spoke to them secretly in secret﴾.

Know that these verses indicate that the stages of his call were three. He began with counsel in private, and they dealt with him by the four matters mentioned. Then he turned to public proclamation. When this had no effect, he combined proclamation and secret speech. The word ﴿thumma﴾ (then) indicates that some of these stages were separated from one another, either in terms of time or in terms of rank, since open proclamation is more severe than secret speech, and combining secret and open speech is more severe than open proclamation alone. If it is asked: with what is ﴿jihaaran﴾ (openly) in the accusative? We say: there are several views:

The first is that it is governed by ﴿da'awtuhum﴾ (I called them) as an absolute object (naṣb al-maṣdar), since calling (duʿa') has as one of its kinds open proclamation (jihar), so it is put in the accusative by it, like ﴿qurfusa﴾ (crouching) with ﴿qa'ada﴾ (sat), because it is one of the kinds of sitting.

The second is that the meaning intended by ﴿da'awtuhum﴾ is ﴿jahartuhum﴾ (I openly addressed them).

The third is that it is an adjective of the verbal noun of ﴿da'a﴾, meaning a calling ﴿jihaaran﴾, that is, openly declared with it.

The fourth is that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning openly declared.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And indeed, every time I have called them, that You might forgive them﴾.

Therefore, when he commanded them to worship, he said: ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾. Know also that when he, peace be upon him, called them, they dealt with him in four ways:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾, meaning that they went so far in imitation (taqlid) that they put their fingers in their ears, so that they would not hear the proof (hujjah) and the clear evidence (bayyinah).

The second: among the verses is this verse, and among them His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings﴾; ﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them﴾; ﴿And that if they had remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾; ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out﴾; ﴿and will provide for him from where he does not expect﴾; ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132].

The third: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 56]. So when they occupy themselves with achieving the goal, what they need in this world is obtained as a consequence.

The fourth: 'Umar went out to seek rain (istisqa') and did nothing more than seek forgiveness. He was asked: "We did not see you seek rain," and he said: "I sought rain with the mijadih of the sky." And from Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah: "The people with the most sins are those who seek forgiveness least, and the people who seek forgiveness most are those with the fewest sins." And from al-Hasan: a man complained to him of drought, and he said: "Seek forgiveness from Allah." Another complained to him of poverty, another of having few children, another of poor yield from his land, and he commanded them all to seek forgiveness. Some of the people said to him: "Men came to you complaining of various kinds of need, and you commanded them all to seek forgiveness?" So he recited to him the verse.

Here there are questions:

The first: Noah, peace be upon him, had before this verse commanded the disbelievers to worship, be God-fearing and obey. What is the benefit of commanding them after that to seek forgiveness? (The answer): When he commanded them to worship, they said to him: "If the old religion we were upon is true, why do you command us to abandon it? And if it is false, how would He accept us after we have disobeyed Him?" Noah, peace be upon him, said: "Even though you have disobeyed Him, nevertheless seek forgiveness from Him for those sins, for indeed He, glorified is He, is ever Forgiving."

The second question: Why did He say ﴿indeed, He is ever Forgiving﴾ and not say "indeed, He is Forgiving"? We say: the meaning is that He has always been Forgiving toward everyone who seeks His forgiveness, as if He is saying: do not think that His forgiving nature has only just come into being; rather He has always been thus, so this is His craft and His practice.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 71, verses 11–13:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ ﴿and provide you with wealth and children, and make for you gardens and make for you rivers﴾.

Know that people are naturally inclined to love immediate benefits (*al-khayrat al-'ajilah*), and for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And another you love: help from God and a near victory﴾ [al-Saff: 13].

[Page 123]

So God, exalted is He, informed them here that their faith in God combines for them, along with a generous share in the Hereafter, fertility and wealth in this world.

The things He promised them of the benefits of this world in this verse are five.

The first: His saying, ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾. Regarding "the sky" there are several interpretations:

One: the rain descends from it to the clouds.

Two: that "the sky" is intended to mean the clouds.

Three: that "the sky" is intended to mean the rain, from the line of poetry:

"When the rain (*al-sama'*) falls on the land of a people, we graze our herds there, even if they are angry."

*Al-midrar* means that which pours down abundantly. *Mif'al* is a pattern (*mif'al*, an intensive form) in which the masculine and feminine are equal, like their saying: a man or a woman who is *mi'tar* (very fragrant) and *mithqal* (very heavy).

The second: His saying, ﴿and provide you with wealth﴾. This is not restricted to one kind of wealth but includes all of it.

The third: His saying, ﴿and children﴾. There is no doubt that this is something the natural disposition inclines toward.

The fourth: His saying, ﴿and make for you gardens﴾, that is, orchards (*basatin*).

The fifth: His saying, ﴿and make for you rivers﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: that "hope" (*al-raja'*) here means fear. From this is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"When the bees sting him, he does not hope for their sting."

*Al-waqar* is greatness, and *al-tawqir* is honouring. From this is His saying: ﴿and honour him﴾. The meaning is: "What is the matter with you that you do not fear God's greatness?" In my view this opinion is not permissible, because "hope" is the opposite of "fear" in the widely transmitted and manifest language. If we were to say that the word "hope" in the language is established to mean "fear," that would be giving preference to a report transmitted by solitary narrators (*ahad*) over a report transmitted by mass transmission (*tawatur*). This leads to undermining the Qur'an, for there is no word in it that could not, by this method, have its negation made into affirmation and its affirmation made into negation.

The second opinion: what is mentioned by the author of *al-Kashshaf*, namely that the meaning of "What is the matter with you" is: "you do not expect to honour God," that is, to glorify Him. And the meaning of "What is the matter with you" is: "you are not in a state in which you contemplate God's glorification of you." "For God" is an explanation of the one who is honoured; had it been placed later, it would have been related to *al-waqar* (dignity).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He has created you in stages﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as if He said: "What is the matter with you that you do not believe in God while this is the state?" This state requires faith in Him. ﴿And He has created you in stages﴾, that is, in successive phases (*taratin*). He first created you from dust, then created you as a drop (*nutfan*), then created you as a clinging clot (*'alaqan*), then created you as a lump of flesh (*mudghan*), then created you as bones and flesh, then brought you forth as another creation.

In my view there is a third opinion: that the people used to belittle Noah, peace be upon him, excessively, so God, exalted is He, commanded them to honour him and to stop belittling him. It is as if He said to them: "If you honour Noah and stop belittling him, that is for the sake of God. So what is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity and do not bring it about for the sake of God and for the sake of His command and obedience? For everything a person does for God's sake, he must hope for good from it."

A fourth opinion: that *al-waqar* here means steadfastness (*al-thabat*), from *waqara* when it became firm and settled. It is as if He said: ﴿What is the matter with you?﴾ At this point the sentence is complete. Then He said, in the form of a question meaning denial: ﴿do not hope for steadfastness from God?﴾ That is, you do not expect God to be steadfast and enduring. For if you expected His steadfastness and permanence, you would fear Him, and you would not have proceeded to belittle His messengers and His commands. The meaning of His saying ﴿you hope﴾ is "you believe," because the one who hopes for a thing believes in it.

Know that when He commanded, in this verse, the glorification of Allah, He argued for the Oneness of Allah (tawhid) by several kinds of proof:

The first: His saying, ﴿Although He has created you in stages﴾. On this there are two views.

The first: Al-Layth said: *al-tawrah* (the stage) means a turn, that is, one state after another, as we mentioned, that he was a drop of fluid, then a clinging clot, up to the last of the stages.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-tawr* means the state, and the meaning is that He created you as kinds that differ, none of you resembling another. Having mentioned this proof for the Oneness of Allah from within the self (anfus), he followed it with the proof for the Oneness of Allah from the horizons (afaq), in keeping with the customary pattern found throughout the Qur'an.

The second proof for the Oneness of Allah is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon therein a light, and made the sun a lamp?﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, sometimes begins with proofs from the self and then with proofs from the horizons, as in this verse. This is because a person's own self is the nearest of things to him, so He rightly began with the nearest. And at other times He begins with proofs from the horizons and then with proofs from the self. This is either because the proofs from the horizons are more manifest and greater, so the beginning with them is for this reason; or because the proofs from the self are present and a sensible person has no need to reflect upon them, whereas what needs reflection is the proofs from the horizons, since doubts about them are more numerous, so the beginning with them is fitting.

Here there are questions.

The first question: His saying, ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾, requires that some of them lie upon others, and this requires that there be no gaps between them. How then do the angels dwell in them? (Answer): The angels are spirits, so perhaps what is meant by their being in layers is that they are parallel, not that they are touching.

The second question: How does He say, ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾, when the moon is not within all of them but only in the lowest heaven? (Answer): This is like saying, "The sultan is in Iraq," where it is not meant that his person is present in every part of Iraq, but that his person is in one region among the regions of Iraq. So it is likewise here.

The third question: The lamp's light is accidental, and the moon's light is accidental and variable, so comparing the moon to a lamp is more fitting than comparing the sun to it. (Answer): Night is an expression for the shadow of the earth, and since the sun is the cause of the removal of the earth's shadow, it resembles a lamp. Also, a lamp has a *diya'* (radiance), and radiance is stronger than *nur* (light). So He assigned the weaker to the moon and the stronger to the sun. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [Yunus: 5].

The second proof for the Oneness of Allah is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon therein a light, and made the sun a lamp?﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, sometimes begins with proofs from the self and then with proofs from the horizons, as in this verse. This is because a person's own self is the nearest of things to him, so He rightly began with the nearest. And at other times He begins with proofs from the horizons and then with proofs from the self. This is either because the proofs from the horizons are more manifest and greater, so the beginning with them is for this reason; or because the proofs from the self are present and a sensible person has no need to reflect upon them, whereas what needs reflection is the proofs from the horizons, since doubts about them are more numerous, so the beginning with them is fitting.

Here there are questions.

The first question: His saying, ﴿seven heavens in layers﴾, requires that some of them lie upon others, and this requires that there be no gaps between them. How then do the angels dwell in them? (Answer): The angels are spirits, so perhaps what is meant by their being in layers is that they are parallel, not that they are touching.

The second question: How does He say, ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾, when the moon is not within all of them but only in the lowest heaven? (Answer): This is like saying, "The sultan is in Iraq," where it is not meant that his person is present in every part of Iraq, but that his person is in one region among the regions of Iraq. So it is likewise here.

The third question: The lamp's light is accidental, and the moon's light is accidental and variable, so comparing the moon to a lamp is more fitting than comparing the sun to it. (Answer): Night is an expression for the shadow of the earth, and since the sun is the cause of the removal of the earth's shadow, it resembles a lamp. Also, a lamp has a *diya'* (radiance), and radiance is stronger than *nur* (light). So He assigned the weaker to the moon and the stronger to the sun. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [Yunus: 5].

Know that He, exalted is He, here returns to the proofs from the self (dalail al-anfus), and this is like an explanation of His saying: ﴿He created you in stages﴾. For He has made clear that He, exalted is He, created them from the earth, then will return them to it, then will bring them out from it once more. As for His saying: ﴿Allah has caused you to grow from the earth like a growth﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: concerning this verse there are two views.

One of them: the meaning of His saying ﴿caused you to grow from the earth﴾ is: He caused your father to grow from the earth, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the example of Jesus in the sight of Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59].

The second: that He, exalted is He, caused all of them to grow from the earth, because He, exalted is He, only creates us from drops of semen, and these are produced from nourishment, which is produced from plants, which are produced from the earth.

The second issue: It would have been expected to say: "He caused you to grow [with] a [remarkable] causing (inbatan)." However, He did not say that; rather He said: "He caused you to grow [as] a growth (nabatan)," and the estimate is: "He caused you to grow, so you grew a growth." In this there is a subtle and fine point, which is that if He had said "caused you to grow a causing," the meaning would be "caused you to grow a strange causing." But when He said "caused you to grow a growth," the meaning is "caused you to grow, so you grew a wondrous growth." This second is better, because causing (al-inbat) is an attribute of Allah, exalted is He, and the attribute of Allah is not perceptible to us; so we do not know that that causing is a wondrous, perfect causing except through the information of Allah, exalted is He. This station is the station of establishing the perfection of Allah's power, so it cannot be established by revelation (al-sam'). But when He said "caused you to grow a growth," with the meaning "caused you to grow, so you grew a wondrous, perfect growth," that is a description of the plant as being wondrous and perfect, and the plant's being thus is an observable, perceptible matter, so it is possible to argue by it for the perfection of Allah's power, exalted is He. Thus this is suited to this station.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 71, verses 22–24**

The third category: among their repulsive deeds is His saying, ﴿And they schemed a tremendous scheme﴾ ﴿And they said: Do not abandon your gods, nor abandon Wadd, nor Suwa', nor Yaghuth, nor Ya'uq, nor Nasr﴾ ﴿They have already led many astray; so do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾. On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** "wa-makaru" (and they schemed) is coordinated with "man lam yazid-hu" (those who did not increase him), because the ones followed were those who schemed, and who said to the followers, "Do not abandon." The pronoun in "wa-qalu" (they said) is plural, though it refers back to "man," because it carries the sense of the plural.

**The second issue:** It is read "kubbaran" and "kubaran," with the doubled and the single *ba'*. It is an intensive form of "kabir" (great). The first degree is "kabir," the middle is "kubar" with the single *ba'*, and the highest is "kubbar" with the doubled *ba'*. Its parallels are "jamil," "jamal," and "jammal" (beautiful), "azim," "uzam," and "uzzam" (great), and "tawil," "tuwal," and "tuwwal" (tall).

**The third issue:** The great scheme was that they said to their followers, ﴿Do not abandon Wadd﴾. They prevented the people from monotheism and commanded them to associate others with God. Since monotheism is the greatest of ranks, preventing it is necessarily the greatest of the major sins. For this reason God described it as "kubbar" (great). Those who prefer the science of kalam (theology) over all other sciences argued from this, saying: The command to associate others with God is "kubbar" in ugliness and disgrace, so the command to monotheism and guidance must be "kubbar" in goodness and religion.

**The fourth issue:** God called it "makr" (scheming) only because of the divine status they attributed to these idols, which contained a stratagem that ensured their continued worship of them. It is as if they said: "These idols are your gods, and they were the gods of your forefathers. If you accepted Nuh's words, you would have to acknowledge about yourselves that you were ignorant, misguided, and disbelievers, and about your forefathers that they were the same." Since a person acknowledging this about himself and about all his predecessors, namely their deficiency, deficit, and ignorance, is extremely difficult, the reference to these meanings through the expression "your gods" became a means of turning them away from the religion. Because this speech contained this hidden stratagem, God named their speech "makr."

**Second explanation:** God related of those leaders that they had wealth and children. Perhaps they said to their followers, "Your gods are better than the god of Nuh, because your gods give you wealth and children, while the god of Nuh gives him nothing, since he is poor." By this scheme they turned them away from obeying Nuh. This is similar to the scheming of Pharaoh when he said, ﴿Is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?﴾ (43:51), and said, ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly express himself? Why then are bracelets of gold not cast upon him?﴾ (43:52–53).

**The fifth issue:** Abu Zayd al-Balkhi mentioned in his book refuting the worshippers of idols that the knowledge that this piece of wood, carved at this moment, does not create the heavens, the earth, the plants, or the animals is a necessary knowledge (*'ilm daruri*). Necessary knowledge does not permit disagreement among rational people about it. The worship of idols was a religion that existed before the coming of Nuh, peace be upon him, as indicated by this verse. That religion has continued until this time, and most of the inhabitants of the far regions of the inhabited world follow it. Therefore it is necessary to interpret this religion in a way whose corruption is not known by the necessity of reason, for otherwise it would not have survived this long a period in most parts of the world. Thus, the adherents of that doctrine must have interpretations:

**First:** Abu Ma'shar Ja'far ibn Muhammad the astrologer said: This doctrine arose only from the doctrine of those who hold that God is a body and in a place. They said that God is light, the greatest of lights, and that the angels who surround the Throne, which is His place, are small lights in comparison with that greatest light. Those who adopted this doctrine made an idol, the greatest of the idols, in the image of their god whom they believed in. They also made idols of varying size, rank, and lowliness in the form of the angels brought near (to God), and they occupied themselves with worshipping those idols, believing that they worshipped God and the angels. Thus the religion of idol worship emerged from the belief in anthropomorphism (*tajsim*).

**Second:** The Sabians (*al-Sabi'a*) believed that the Supreme God created these fixed and wandering stars and entrusted the management of this lower world to them. Humans are thus slaves of these stars, and the stars are slaves of the Supreme God. Therefore humans must worship the stars. Then, since these stars would rise at one time and set at another, they made idols in their likenesses and occupied themselves with worshipping them, and their aim was the worship of the stars.

**Third:** The people of ancient times were astrologers according to the doctrine of the adherents of judicial astrology (*ashab al-ahkam*), who attributed the good fortunes and misfortunes of this world to the stars. When a wondrous configuration occurred in the heavens that was suitable for a wondrous talisman (*tilsam*), they would make that talisman. Remarkable states and great effects would appear from it. They would glorify it, honor it, and occupy themselves with worshipping it. They would make each talisman in a form corresponding to a specific star and a specific zodiacal sign. It was said that Wadd was in the form of a man, Suwa' in the form of a woman, Yaghuth in the form of a lion, Ya'uq in the form of a horse, and Nasr in the form of an eagle.

**Fourth:** Righteous peoples would die, and they would make images in their likeness and occupy themselves with glorifying them. Their aim was to glorify those peoples who had died, so that they would be intercessors for them before God. This is what is meant by their saying: ﴿We worship them only so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ (39:3).

**Fifth:** Perhaps a great king or a great person would die, and they would make an image of his likeness and look at it. Those who came after them thought that their forefathers had worshipped these images, so they occupied themselves with worshipping them by imitating their forefathers. Or perhaps these five names, namely Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr, were the names of five of the sons of Adam. When they died, Iblis said to those who came after them: "If you make their images, you will look at them." They did so. When those died, he said to those who came after them: "They used to worship them," and so they worshipped them. For this reason the Messenger, peace be upon him, first forbade visiting graves, then permitted it, according to what is narrated, that he, peace be upon him, said: "I had forbidden you from visiting graves. Now visit them, for in visiting them there is a reminder."

**Sixth:** Those who say that God is a body, and that movement and indwelling are permissible for Him, do not find it unlikely that God would indwell the person of a human being or the person of an idol. When they perceive a remarkable state from that idol made in the manner of a talisman, it occurs to them that God has entered that idol. For this reason, a group of the early Rafidah (*al-Rafidah*), when they saw that Ali, peace be upon him, uprooted the gate of Khaybar, which was contrary to the usual, said: "God has entered his body, and he is God."

**Seventh:** Perhaps they took those idols as a prayer niche (*mihrab*), while their intended object of worship was God.

This is the sum of what is in this chapter. Some of it is false by the evidence of reason. For when it is established that God is not a body, the making of an idol in the form of God is invalidated, and the claim of indwelling and descent is also invalidated. When it is established that God is the one capable of all things, the claim of intermediaries and talismans is invalidated. And when the Law has come with the prohibition of making idols, the claim of taking them as prayer niches and intercessors is invalidated.

**The sixth issue:** These five idols were the greatest of their idols. Then they moved from the people of Nuh to the Arabs. Wadd belonged to the tribe of Kalb, Suwa' to Hamdan, Yaghuth to Madhhij, Ya'uq to Murad, and Nasr to Himyar. For this reason the Arabs named their children 'Abd Wadd and 'Abd Yaghuth. This is what has been said in the books. But there is a difficulty in this, because the world was destroyed in the time of the Flood. How then did those idols survive, and how did they move to the Arabs? It cannot be said that Nuh, peace be upon him, placed them in the ark and preserved them, because he, peace be upon him, came to abolish and smash them. How, then, can it be said that he placed them in the ark out of eagerness to preserve them?

**The seventh issue:** It is read "la tadharunna Wuddan" with a *fatha* on the *waw* and with a *damma* on the *waw*. Al-Layth said: "Wadd" with a *fatha* on the *waw* is an idol that belonged to the people of Nuh, while "Wudd" with a *damma* is an idol of the Quraysh, and 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wadd was named after it. I say: According to al-Layth's statement, it must not be permissible here to read "Wudd" with a *damma*, because these verses are about the story of Nuh, not the condition of the Quraysh. Al-A'mash read "wa-la Yaghuthan wa-Ya'uqan" with *tanwin* (nunation, i.e., *sarf*). This is a problematic reading, because if they are Arabic or foreign names, there are two reasons for their being diptote (*mamnu' min al-sarf*): either definiteness together with the pattern of a verb, or definiteness together with foreignness. Perhaps he gave them *tanwin* because he found their sisters (similar names) declined: Wuddan, Suwa'an, and Nasran.

Know that when Nuh related what they said to their followers, ﴿Do not abandon your gods﴾, he said: ﴿They have already led many astray﴾. Regarding this there are two possibilities:

**The first:** Those leaders "have already led many astray" before these ones who enjoined the worship of idols. And this was not the first time they had occupied themselves with misguidance.

**The second:** The pronoun may refer to the idols, as in His saying: ﴿They have indeed led many of the people astray﴾ (14:36). On this view, the idols are treated like human beings, as in His saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which to walk?﴾ (7:195).

As for His saying, ﴿so do not increase the wrongdoers except in error﴾, there are two questions about it:

**The first question:** What is the position of His saying, "so do not increase the wrongdoers"? (The answer:) It is as if Nuh, peace be upon him, when he had lengthily enumerated their repugnant deeds and their ugly words, his heart filled with rage and anger against them, so he concluded his speech by invoking a curse upon them.

**The second question:** He was sent only to turn them away from error, so how is it fitting for him to pray to God that He increase their error? (The answer is) on two grounds:

**The first:** Perhaps the intended error is not error in religious matters but error in their worldly affairs, and in the promotion of their scheming and their stratagems.

**The second:** "Error" here means punishment, according to His saying: ﴿Indeed the criminals are in error and madness﴾ (54:47).

Then, after God related the speech of Nuh, peace be upon him, He said after it: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire﴾. On this there are issues:

**The first issue:** "ma" (what) is a *silah* (redundant, extra particle), as in His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of the covenant﴾ (4:155) and ﴿So by a mercy from God﴾ (3:159). The meaning is "from their sins," that is, "for their sake and because of them." Ibn Mas'ud read: "min khati'atihim ma ughriqu" (with "ma" placed after the word "khati'at"). According to this reading, "ma" is not an extra particle, because "ma" together with what follows it forms a verbal noun (*masdar*).

The second: that they will become so.

Know that when he, peace be upon him, invoked (judgment) upon the disbelievers, he then said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾, meaning: for what proceeded from me of leaving what is better. It is also possible that when he invoked against the disbelievers, he did so only because of the harm he suffered from them, so that invocation against them was like taking revenge, and so he sought forgiveness for that, because it contained a seeking of the self's own portion.

Then he said: (and to my parents). His father was Lamech ibn Methuselah, and his mother was Shamkha bint Anush, and both were believers. Ata' said: there was no disbeliever among Noah's ancestors between him and Adam, peace be upon them both, and there were ten fathers between him and Adam. Al-Hasan ibn Ali recited "wa-liwaladayya," meaning Sam and Ham.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever enters my house as a believer﴾. It was said: "My house" means my mosque. It was said: my ship. It was said: whoever enters my religion. If it is objected: according to this interpretation, His saying "as a believer" becomes repetitive, we answer: whoever enters His religion outwardly may be a believer in his heart, and may not be. The meaning is: whoever enters my religion with the affirmation of the heart.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for the believing men and the believing women﴾. He first specified Himself in the supplication, then those connected to Him, because they are more deserving and more entitled to His supplication. Then He generalized to the believing men and believing women.

Then He concluded the speech once more with a supplication against the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction﴾. That is, ruin and annihilation. Everything that is destroyed is said to be "tabar" (perished), and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are doomed (mutabbar) in what they are engaged in﴾ [al-A'raf: 139], and His saying: ﴿And to destroy what they had mastered with complete destruction (tatbir)﴾ [al-Isra: 7]. So Allah answered his supplication and destroyed them entirely. If it is asked: what was the offense of the children when they were drowned? The answer has several aspects:

First: Allah the Exalted dried up the loins of their fathers and made the wombs of their women barren forty or ninety years before the flood, so there were no children with them when they were drowned. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Seek forgiveness from your Lord… and He will increase you in wealth and sons﴾, and this indicates by implication that if they did not seek forgiveness, He would not increase them with sons.

Second: al-Hasan said: Allah knew the innocence of the children, so He destroyed them without punishment.

Third: They drowned along with them, not as a form of punishment, but just as they die by drowning and burning; and this was an increase in the punishment of the fathers and mothers when they saw their children drowning. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may His blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, the Prophet, and his family and companions all together.
